sentences.text: This prehistoric shark is sometimes called the pygmy white shark.
It belongs to the class Chondrichthyes, which includes cartilaginous fish like sharks and rays.
Most researchers place it in the family Cretoxyrhinidae.
The genus currently includes only one valid species, P. orientalis.
Its teeth were triangular and compressed, featuring irregular serrations with small serrate lateral cusplets.
Individual teeth could reach a length of about 3 to 6 centimeters.
Some teeth found in Volgograd, Russia, lack serrations and are classified as Palaeocarcharodon cf. orientalis.
The exact size of the animal remains uncertain.
It is estimated to have been comparable in size to mako sharks or modern great white sharks.
Fossil evidence consists of a few possible vertebrae and several teeth.
Remains have been found in the Americas, Asia, Russia, North Africa, and Europe.
The genus Palaeocarcharodon was named by Casier in 1960.
Sinzow originally named the species Carcharodon orientalis in 1899.
The type species of the genus is Carcharodon orientalis.
Palaeocarcharodon landanensis has been proposed as a synonym of Carcharodon orientalis.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Palaeocarcharodon as Otodontidae.
Palaeocarcharodon lived between 61.7 and 55.8 million years ago during the Middle Paleocene and Early Eocene.
The classification of Palaeocarcharodon remains a subject of debate among researchers.
In 2013, some researchers suggested that P. landanensis is a senior synonym of P. orientalis, though this is still debated.
While some theories placed Palaeocarcharodon in the family Otodontidae, recent papers generally classify it in Cretoxyrhinidae.
